title: some and any
subtitle: some flowers / any flowers
summary: Use some in positive sentences and any in negative ones, choose between them in questions, and use any to mean 'it doesn't matter which'.

left.label: some (positive)
examples: He's busy. He has **some** work to do.

right.label: any (negative)
examples: He's lazy. He never does **any** work.

lesson.heading: any when the meaning is negative
lesson.text: We also use **any** in sentences that are not negative in form but negative in meaning - after **without**, **refuse** and **hardly**, for example.

examples.note: = she didn't take any money with her

examples.text: It's a very easy exam. Hardly **anybody** fails.

left.label: some in questions
left.text: When we think the person or thing exists, and when we ask for or offer things.

right.label: any in questions
right.text: In most questions - we don't know if the person or thing exists.
examples: Have you seen **any** good films recently?

lesson.heading: if + any
lesson.text: We use **any** after **if**, and in sentences that have the idea of *if*.

examples.text: Let me know if you need **anything**.
If anyone has **any** questions, I'll be pleased to answer them.
I'm sorry for **any** trouble I've caused.
examples.note: = if I have caused any trouble

examples.text: The police want to speak to **anyone** who saw the accident.

lesson.heading: any = it doesn't matter which
lesson.text: **Any** (and **anybody / anyone / anything / anywhere**) can also mean *it doesn't matter which*.

examples.text: You can take **any** bus. They all go to the centre.
Come and see me **any** time you want.
We forgot to lock the door. **Anybody** could have come in.
*A:* What would you like? *B:* I don't mind. **Anything**.
*A:* Where shall we go? *B:* **Anywhere**. I just want to go out.

lesson.heading: somebody, anybody + they
lesson.text: **Somebody / someone / anybody / anyone** are singular words, so the verb is singular. But we normally use **they / them / their** after them.

examples.text: If anybody wants to leave early, **they** can.

lesson.text: If you can put not in the sentence, you almost always need any; if the sentence is positive or you are offering something, use some.

exercises.explanation: The sentence is negative (didn't), so we use any.

exercises.prompt: I was too surprised to say ___.
exercises.explanation: Too surprised to say = I didn't say anything, so the meaning is negative.

exercises.prompt: There's ___ at the door. Can you go and see who it is?
exercises.explanation: A positive sentence about a person we know is there: somebody/someone.

exercises.prompt: You must be hungry. Why don't I get you ___ to eat?
exercises.explanation: We use something in questions when we offer things.

exercises.prompt: Does each sentence need some or any in the gap (shown as ...)?

items.text: Tonight I'm going out with ... friends of mine.
Have you seen ... good movies recently?
I'd like ... information about what there is to see in this town.
You can use your card to withdraw money at ... cash machine.
Those apples look nice. Shall we get ...?
If there are ... words you don't understand, look them up in a dictionary.

exercises.prompt: There was hardly ___ on the beach. It was almost deserted.
exercises.explanation: Hardly anybody = almost nobody, so the meaning is negative.

exercises.prompt: I can't drive and I don't know ___ about cars.
exercises.explanation: A negative sentence (don't know), so we use anything.

exercises.prompt: Let's go away. Let's go ___ warm and sunny.
exercises.explanation: A positive suggestion about a particular kind of place: somewhere.

exercises.prompt: Match each question with the answer that means 'it doesn't matter which'.

pairs.left: Which bus do I have to take?
pairs.right: Any bus. They all go to the centre.
I don't mind. Any day next week will be OK.

pairs.left: What do you want to eat?
Who shall I invite to the party?
pairs.right: It's your party. You can invite anybody you want.
It's up to you. You can sit anywhere you like.

exercises.prompt: I'm going out now. If ___ asks where I am, tell them you don't know.
exercises.explanation: After if we use any-: if anybody asks ...
Correct. Someone takes a singular verb (has), but we use their afterwards.

exercises.prompt: This is a no-parking area. ___ who parks their car here will have to pay a fine.
exercises.explanation: The sentence has the idea of if: if there is anybody who parks here.
